newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland's pension reform under election cloud.
newsitem.headline: Poland's pension reform under election cloud.

text.p: Poland this year faces a reform of its ailing communist-era state pensions system, spurred by soaring costs and forecasts of economic catastrophe unless it radically overhauls current hand-to-mouth arrangements.
The process began last year but most of the crucial decisions have yet to be taken and could prove difficult as parliamentary elections will also be held this year.
The ruling leftist coalition may not want to risk the anger of millions of pensioners who fear change, analysts say.

"I am afraid the reform will be delayed. There are people in the government who want to go ahead with it, but others may block it for political reasons," said Bogdan Wyznikiewicz, an analyst for the private Market Economy Research Institute.
"The election year is the worst time for launching the reform, with both the coalition and the opposition using it for their political ends," he added.

The previous labour minister Andrzej Baczkowski, who died of a heart attack last November after months of stressful work on the pension scheme, had promised to prepare four bills triggering the pension reform by the end of March.

"If we fail to launch the reform quickly, our social security system will collapse... in the next century and an economic catastrophe will follow," Baczkowski said at his last news conference in October.
His successor, Andrzej Zielinski, promises to meet the deadline but many analysts and politicians say the bills, even if approved by the government, are likely to get stuck in parliament.

Under the current system, inherited from the communist era, each retired Pole receives a pension from the state Social Security Office (ZUS), which collects from employers 45 percent of workers' wages and spends the cash on pensions.
This bureaucratic and inefficient system poses a serious threat to public finances, as the number pensioners is set to rise from the current nine million to 11 million in 2010.

The national budget's subsidy for pensions already amounts to more than 20 percent of its revenues annually and the percentage will have to rise steeply, creating an unmanageable budget deficit, unless the reforms are implemented.
The four bills promised by Baczkowski include two pivotal ones -- to create new, privately managed pension funds and to endowing the funds with the shares of privatised firms.
Under the reform plan, each eligible Pole would get their pension from three sources rather than only from ZUS.
The first, and at first the biggest, part of a person's pension would still come from ZUS, the operations of which would be rationalised.

As of 1998, ZUS would start monitoring each worker's contribution and base his or her future pension on the size of premiums and duration of employment, replacing the current complicated system of calculating pensions.
The second part of the pension would come from new, privately-managed pension funds, to be set up in the next several years.
The funds, under close government supervision, would compulsorily receive part of the premium now paid to ZUS and invest their capital in safe securities.

People currently of school age or slightly older would be obliged to start paying premiums to the funds. Older workers, who are below 50 years of age, would be free to choose whether to join the funds or rely only on ZUS.
The funds' capital is to be strengthened with shares of companies undergoing privatisation, but details of the scheme still remain undecided.
The government has said the funds were likely to receive minority stakes in companies with good financial results, such as the telecommunications giant TPSA, distilleries and banks.
Under a different proposal, earnings from privatisations would go to ZUS to compensate it for the loss of that part of premiums that would go to new funds.
Private sector funds and insurance companies would be the third source of pensions and the government would offer tax relief to people saving with them.

The first bill, initiating the social security reform, was approved by parliament last year. It curbs annual increases in pensions by pegging them to a basket of consumer goods prices rather than to average wage growth in the economy.

Foreign analysts say pension reform is a great opportunity for the economy as the new pension funds would help deepen capital and financial markets to cope with the investment inflows associated with accession to the European Union, which Poland hopes to join in or soon after 2000.
